subtechniques.name: Anonymous swapping service
subtechniques.description: From an anonymized browser (such as Tor Browser), use a non-KYC (Know Your Customer) service swapping service (see Appendix A8: Crypto Swapping Services without Registration and KYC) and convert your Monero to BTC and transfer those to the BTC Wallet you have on your anonymized VM. You should now have an anonymized Bitcoin wallet that can be used for purchasing services that do not accept Monero. You should never access this wallet from a non-anonymized environment. Always use well-thought OPSEC with your BTC transactions. Remember those can be traced back to you.

subtechniques.name: Avoid convertion to actual currency
subtechniques.description: Because this will require KYC-practices which breaks the anonymity.

subtechniques.name: Avoid linking phone numbers to crypto platforms
subtechniques.description: Phone numbers (SIM cards) are tied to identities. Linking them to cryptocurrency platforms could contribute to de-anonymization and should therefore be avoided.

subtechniques.name: Avoid reuse of wallet addresses
subtechniques.description: Cryptocurrency transactions are conducted on a public ledger, which could be traced. When using the same addresses multiple times, transactions could be traces back to you more easily. Avoiding reusing wallet addresses reduces tying transactions together.

subtechniques.name: Avoid sending crypto directly from exchange to DNM
subtechniques.description: Cryptocurrency transactions are public on the blockchain and if you use an exchange they have personal information about you. Conducting direct transactions to Darknet markets could therefore de-anonymize you.

subtechniques.name: Desktop wallets
subtechniques.description: Desktop wallets:The desktop wallets are softwares that you have to download and locally execute on your computer. The desktop wallets provide you with complete control over your funds and keys. As you generate a new desktop wallet, a file named “wallet.dat” gets stored locally on your desktop. This file stores the private key information that will be used to access your crypto addresses. Thus, it requires encryption with a personal password. You need to keep the files safe and not let others access them.

subtechniques.name: Hardware wallet
subtechniques.description:
Hardware or ‘cold’ wallets (extra layer of protection by keeping private keys offline and away from online threats). Hardware wallets: The hardware wallets, as the name suggests, are physical, electronic devices that use a random number generator (RNG) for generating both private and public keys. Then the keys are stored in the device itself, which does not need an internet connection for storage. This implies that the hardware wallets are cold wallets and finds its mention as one of the most secure alternatives. These wallets offer a high level of security as compared to their counterparts from the online attacks. 

However, they may possess a threat if the firmware implementation does not take place properly. Additionally, the hardware wallets tend to be usually less user-friendly, making it difficult to access the funds compared to the hot wallets. The hardware wallets are the best option if you hold a large amount of crypto and that too for a long time. You need to set up a PIN along with a recovery phrase to protect your device. These will help you in case your wallet gets lost.

subtechniques.name: Paper wallets
subtechniques.description:
Paper wallers: Paper wallets can be termed as pieces of paper on which you usually note down the crypto address and its private key. They are physically printed in the form of QR codes, after which these codes can be scanned for executing cryptocurrency transactions. Some of the paper wallet websites permit you to download their code for generating new addresses and keys while they remain offline. This makes sure that the wallets are highly resistant to online hacking attacks and probably are alternatives to cold storage. However, now the paper wallets are considered dangerous, owing to potential threats.

subtechniques.name: Stealth addresses
subtechniques.description: imagine getting a new email address every time you receive a message. That's how stealth addresses work in privacy coins. Monero (XMR), one of the best privacy coins, uses this method effectively. It generates a one-time public address for each transaction, a private view key to see incoming funds, and a private spend key for sending money. This makes tracking individual transactions nearly impossible.

subtechniques.name: Web wallets
subtechniques.description: Web wallets: The web wallets can be used to access the blockchains via a browser interface without the requirement of installation or downloading. The web wallets include both the exchange wallets and the other browser oriented wallet providers. In most instances, you can create a new wallet and set your personal password for accessing it. But, some of the service providers do hold and manage the private key, which could be dangerous. Now, most web wallets enable you to secure your cryptocurrency by holding and managing your private keys.

subtechniques.name: zk-SNARKs
subtechniques.description:
zk-SNARKs is like a magic trick. It proves a transaction is legitimate without revealing any specifics about it. Zcash, a pioneer among the best crypto privacy coins, uses zk-SNARKs to keep transaction details under wraps while still verifying their validity.

These techniques highlight how privacy coins like Monero, Zcash, and others offer enhanced privacy and security. Each method contributes to making transactions anonymous and untraceable, positioning these currencies as some of the best crypto privacy coins available.
